newsitem.title: GERMANY: EU trade unfazed by gene maize protest in Germany.
newsitem.headline: EU trade unfazed by gene maize protest in Germany.

text.p: EU maize markets ignored protests by environmental group Greenpeace over the shipment of U.S. feed maize, believed to contain genetically-altered strains, to the Czech republic via Germany, traders said.
"U.S. maize (corn) shipments to the EU are only beginning to be made up of new crop and are down from last year anyway," one said.
"By the time the debate over genetic modification affects maize imports, the EU will have decided how to handle them."
"I cannot imagine them denying U.S. maize entrance into the EU because it would cause a major bilateral trade row."

The EU Commission is due to decide on December 18 whether to allow imports of modified maize, developed by Swiss chemicals company Ciba Geigy AG and accounting for an estimated 0.6 percent of the 1996/97 U.S. maize crop.
But transit shipments are not prohibited and eastern Europe is in line for more such cargoes as its import tariffs are lower than in the EU.
The EU has harvested an ample feed maize crop of its own this year and mostly restricts use of U.S. corn to the starch industry, where its low moisture content is sought after.
But maize by-product corngluten is widely used in the EU feeds industry.
Greenpeace said it wanted to show concern over possible risks of genetically-altered products was not restricted to the EU.

EU third country maize imports in the 1996/97 season (July/June) totalled 218,000 tonnes on Dec 9 and included shipments to Germany, France, the Netherlands and Britain, farm price office ZMP in Bonn said.
But U.S. maize in that total would have been of the old crop which does not contain gene-altered strains.
The figure described transactions already carried out and others yet to come and did not distinguish between genuine EU consumption and transit.
A year ago, the figure was 1.05 million tonnes, but this included 700,000 tonnes under special Spanish and Portugese GATT arrangements, offering the U.S. market access.
